intro: A flute sings over plucked strings, and the piano answers as gently. Inside this D♭-major slow movement, Tchaikovsky hides a fast dance built around a French song his brothers used to sing.

sections.label: A · Flute over plucked strings
sections.mNote: The D♭-major melody passes from flute to piano

sections.label: B · Fast piano and a French song
sections.mNote: The Prestissimo begins in F major

sections.label: A′ · The piano brings the song back
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns with new piano decoration

sections.label: Coda · A quiet D♭-major close
sections.mNote: The oboe completes the tune before the final cadence

cues.title: Flute and plucked strings
cues.text: Plucked strings make a quiet space for the flute’s D♭-major melody. The piano takes the tune next. After the first movement’s huge opening chords, the soloist arrives here almost as another woodwind.
cues.evidence: Second-movement opening and solo handover: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky). Tonic Chord identifies flute bars 5–12 and piano bars 13–20: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two pianos before the orchestra
cues.text: By 2 January 1875, Tchaikovsky has completed the concerto’s two-piano arrangement. Three days later he plays the work to Nikolay Rubinstein and Nikolay Hubert. The full orchestral score still lies ahead.
cues.evidence: Manuscript date 21 December 1874/2 January 1875; private play-through 24 December/5 January; orchestration completed 9/21 February. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: The piano slips into a dance
cues.text: The Prestissimo starts in F major with quick piano writing. Soon the strings take a new tune in D major, and the pianist becomes their accompanist. A miniature scherzo has slipped into the middle of the slow movement.
cues.evidence: Second-movement middle section, keys and scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); formal outline at https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The brothers’ French song
cues.text: The fast middle borrows Il faut s’amuser, danser et rire — one must have fun, dance and laugh. Modest Tchaikovsky remembers singing it constantly with his brother Anatoly in the early 1870s. Their brother puts the refrain into a piano concerto.
cues.evidence: Modest Tchaikovsky, The Life of Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, vol. 1 (1900), p. 466, quoted under Related Works. The tune is by Jean-Baptiste-Edouard Montaubry. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: The piano remembers the flute
cues.text: The opening melody returns in D♭ major, now in the piano and dressed in small ornaments. The oboe continues it. The fast dance is over, and the flute’s first tune has become a conversation.
cues.evidence: Second-movement reprise: ornamented piano theme followed by oboe, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three pianissimos in D♭
cues.text: The coda settles quietly in D♭ major. Its last cadence moves from G♭ major to D♭, marked ppp: a gentle answer to the first movement’s closing chords.
cues.evidence: The second movement ends ppp with a plagal cadence in D♭ major. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: An F-major chord starts running
transitions.to: B · Fast piano and a French song
transitions.how: The piano holds a high F-major chord, pianissimo, at the end of the quiet section. The Prestissimo begins in that same key with fast solo writing. The strings then introduce the French song in D major over the piano’s accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: High F-major chord, Prestissimo opening and D-major string tune: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: The piano returns to D♭
transitions.from: B · Fast piano and a French song
transitions.to: A′ · The piano brings the song back
transitions.how: A cadenza-like piano passage ends the fast episode. The soloist brings back the opening D♭-major melody at the slower tempo, adding ornaments to the line first sung by the flute.
transitions.evidence: Tonic Chord identifies the solo link in bars 135–145 and the D♭-major return at bar 146. https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/

transitions.title: The oboe completes the tune
transitions.from: A′ · The piano brings the song back
transitions.how: The oboe continues the returning melody and resolves it in D♭ major. A brief coda follows, ending with a G♭-major chord moving to D♭, marked ppp.
transitions.evidence: Oboe continuation, tonic resolution and plagal close: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
